title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?

paper.title: Does self-distillation improve reasoning?
paper.abstract:
Abstract Self-distillation is an emerging approach that trains a model to imitate its own predictions when conditioned on privileged information, such as correct answers or environmental feedback. Recent methods have reported better sample efficiency and generalization than reinforcement learning (RL), but it remains unclear whether these gains extend beyond in-distribution evaluations and whether they stem from privileged distillation. In this paper, we revisit two representative methods, Self-Distillation Policy Optimization (SDPO) and On-Policy Self-Distillation (OPSD), across code, science, tool use, and math reasoning tasks. We find that their reported gains do not consistently generalize to unseen problems and are largely explained by overfitting or transferring existing reasoning behavior, rather than effectively using privileged information. Moreover, self-distillation gradients show weak alignment with policy gradients that directly optimize expected reward, questioning whether they provide an effective direction for policy improvement. Our experiments across Qwen3 models (1.7B–14B) and OLMo-3-7B suggest that effectively leveraging privileged information to improve reasoning remains an open challenge.
Our code is available at https://github.com/sleepypandu/does-sd-improve-reasoning .

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Figure 1: SDPO reduces solution diversity on LiveCodeBench v6. AST-unique solutions per training problem (from 8 8 samples) for Qwen3-14B before (Base) and after 200 200 steps of GRPO or SDPO (mean ± \pm std, four seeds). Diversity collapse suggests memorization. Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) has become a standard approach for finetuning large language models (LLMs) on reasoning tasks such as mathematics and coding ( Lambert et al., 2025 ; Guo et al., 2025 ) . As responses in these domains are automatically verifiable, scaling RLVR is straightforward. However, typical RLVR pipelines use binary rewards that indicate only whether the final answer is correct or whether all unit tests pass. Such rewards provide no information on how attempted solutions should be revised. Process reward models score individual reasoning steps ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Cui et al., 2025 ) , but require training additional models. A recently popularized alternative to RLVR is self-distillation, which requires neither an external stronger model nor an explicit reward function. It exploits the fact that reasoning tasks often come with feedback far richer than the binary outcome that RLVR consumes, such as reference solutions, critiques, error messages, or failing unit tests. In self-distillation, the model samples a trace and is trained to match, at each token along that trace, the distribution of a (teacher) copy of itself that additionally conditions on this privileged information ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ; Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ) . The self-conditioned teacher converts rich but unstructured feedback into a dense, per-token training signal. However, prior work questions the validity of self-distillation objectives as a mechanism to improve the student policy. The self-conditioned teacher’s outputs do not express uncertainty through tokens such as “wait”, “hmmm”, and “perhaps,” so training against it suppresses the model’s ability to correct past mistakes as it reasons and shortens the student’s traces in ways that hurt performance ( Kim et al., 2026 ; Pan et al., 2026 ; Kaur et al., 2026 ) . Moreover, the self-conditioned teacher is unable to consistently distinguish between correct and incorrect student generations ( Harne et al., 2026 ; Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . Together, these results raise a more fundamental question: does self-distillation extract useful guidance from privileged information, or are its reported gains driven by simpler mechanisms? Figure 2: The reference solution barely changes the self-distillation teacher. Teacher log-probabilities (thinking on) along a Qwen3-8B thinking-off student rollout on an OpenThoughts problem, with the problem’s reference solution in context (ref z z , top) and with no solution (no z z , bottom). In each panel, the first row is the sampled token and the three rows below are the student’s next three most likely tokens. The two teachers assign very similar probabilities, suggesting that OPSD distillation effects do not significantly depend on z z ( Section 4.3 ). We revisit this question through careful reproductions of self-distillation policy optimization (SDPO) ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) and on-policy self-distillation (OPSD) ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) . We leverage Qwen3 ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) and Olmo-3 ( Olmo Team, 2025 ) models to ensure our observations hold over a range of model sizes and families. We find that the reported gains from privileged-information self-distillation in reasoning domains are weaker than they appear: • SDPO’s coding gains do not transfer to unseen problems ( Section 4.1 ). SDPO’s LiveCodeBench v6 ( Jain et al., 2024 ) results train and evaluate on the same set of coding problems. Correcting for this reveals that SDPO overfits to its training problems, reducing the diversity of its solutions ( Figure 1 ), and degrades on held-out problems while policy-gradient training on the same verifiable reward generalizes. • SDPO’s gains in science reasoning and tool use do not generalize out of domain ( Section 4.2 ). Across five science-reasoning ( Feng et al., 2024 ) and tool-use ( Tang et al., 2023 ) domains, SDPO and GRPO in-domain performances are similar, but in four of five it lowers accuracy on the held-out domains, while GRPO preserves it. • OPSD transfers thinking-mode behavior, not privileged information ( Section 4.3 ). In math reasoning, privileged information barely changes the self-conditioned teacher’s token distribution ( Figure 2 ), and distilling thinking-mode behavior has a substantially larger effect than privileged information within OPSD’s reported results. • Self-distillation gradients do not align with policy gradients ( Section 4.4 ). Prior work motivates self-distillation as approximate policy improvement by arguing that its gradient aligns with the policy gradient ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . This alignment matters because a small update improves expected reward only to the extent that it follows the policy gradient ( Section 3.1 ). We therefore measure how well each method’s training gradient aligns with the policy gradient on held-out problems. On Qwen3 models, OPSD and SDPO gradients are consistently less aligned than GRPO gradients computed on the same training problems and often point away from the held-out policy gradient altogether.

sections.heading: 2 Related works
sections.text: Reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR). The goal of reinforcement learning is to maximize the expectation of reward under a policy’s responses. For verifiable tasks in math reasoning and coding, such rewards are assigned by verifying the equivalence between expressions or checking whether a proposed program passes all test-cases. RLVR for LLMs is typically done using policy gradient algorithms ( Williams, 1992 ; Sutton et al., 2000 ) . Although PPO ( Schulman et al., 2017 ) was used in foundational work ( Ouyang et al., 2022 ; Bai et al., 2022 ) , critic-free methods such as GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) and RLOO ( Kool et al., 2019 ; Ahmadian et al., 2024 ) have become popular due to their simplicity, despite feedback only being given at the trajectory level. On-policy distillation (OPD). Unlike classic distillation, which tries to match teacher-generated outputs ( Hinton et al., 2015 ) , on-policy distillation seeks to boost performance by minimizing per-token divergences between student logits π θ ( ⋅ | x , y < t ) \pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,y_{<t}) and teacher logits π T ( ⋅ | x , y < t ) \pi_{T}(\cdot|x,y_{<t}) along prefixes sampled from the student policy ( Lu and Thinking Machines Lab, 2025 ; Xu et al., 2026 ; Gu et al., 2023 ) . OPD has been shown to be effective in post-training small-models ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) and merging the capabilities of multiple domain-specialist expert models ( Xu et al., 2026 ; Kimi Team, 2026 ; Ma et al., 2026 ) . Self-distillation and privileged information. Instead of relying on an external stronger model, self-distillation ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ; Zhao et al., 2026a ; Hübotter et al., 2026 ) parameterizes the teacher distribution as π T ( ⋅ | x , y < t ) = π θ ( ⋅ | x , z , y < t ) \pi_{T}(\cdot|x,y_{<t})=\pi_{\theta}(\cdot|x,z,y_{<t}) , with privileged information z z which is derived from a reference solution or environmental feedback. This purportedly moves the student towards a higher-reward policy, transferring the reference solution’s reasoning content. Limitations of self-distillation. Prior work documents several failure modes of self-distillation: SDPO generalizes poorly out of distribution and in continual learning settings ( Wang et al., 2026 ) , self-distillation degrades thinking models by suppressing backtracking behavior and collapsing response lengths ( Kaur et al., 2026 ; Harne et al., 2026 ) , and the self-conditioned teacher fails to distinguish correct from incorrect student solutions ( Nguyen et al., 2026 ) . Concurrently, Shrestha and Tessier (2026) show that OPSD’s gains stem from thinking-mode transfer rather than privileged information. Methods that retain GRPO and use the teacher only to reweight advantages such as Pan et al. (2026) fall outside our scope, as we study the self-distillation objective in isolation. We provide an extended discussion of existing work on the limitations of self-distillation, and of how our paper differs from each, in Appendix A .

4 Experimental results
sections.text: We now examine whether the reported gains of prior self-distillation works reflect the generalization performance of policy gradients ( Section 4.1 ), require reasoning behavior ( Section 4.2 ), transfer via privileged information ( Section 4.3 ), and have gradients that align with the policy gradient as Proposition 3.1 would require of an optimal teacher ( Section 4.4 ).

sections.heading: 4.1 SDPO does not generalize to new coding problems
sections.text: Harne et al. (2026) suggest that the self-conditioned teacher is heavily biased towards the reference solution given in context in a way that does not generalize, which makes the coding gains reported by SDPO ( Hübotter et al., 2026 ) surprising. We observe that SDPO’s coding evaluations reuse its training problems, thus not cleanly measuring generalization. We hypothesize that SDPO’s coding gains stem from this discrepancy. SDPO builds its teacher from privileged information available only at training time. On coding tasks, the teacher sees a successful student rollout from the same batch along with environment feedback on execution errors on test cases. They claim that SDPO improves 7.6 % 7.6\% over GRPO baselines in accuracy on LiveCodeBench v6 ( Jain et al., 2024 ) evaluations. We construct a clean split of the LCB data, reproduce SDPO overall gains on their data split, and observe that SDPO does not lead to performance gains when evaluated on an unseen test set. Figure 3: Qwen3-8B SDPO vs. GRPO on LiveCodeBench v6 across four seeds, scored as the fraction of problems with no failing test cases (mean ± \pm std). train_seen and train_unseen evaluate training problems on seen and on held-out test cases respectively; test_unseen evaluates held-out problems. The 20000 20000 training generations reported by Hübotter et al. (2026) is marked in red. Setup. LiveCodeBench v6 pairs each competitive programming problem with a set of test cases. Concretely, the original work trains on all problems with half of each problem’s test cases removed, and evaluates on the unmodified dataset. To separate memorization from generalization, we instead split the problems into disjoint, equal-size sets 𝒫 train \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{train}} and 𝒫 test \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{test}} , giving three evaluation groups: train_seen (test cases used during training), train_unseen (held-out test cases of problems in 𝒫 train \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{train}} ), and test_unseen (all test cases of problems in 𝒫 test \mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{test}} ). Results. We train Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Olmo-3-7B-Instruct on this split with SDPO and GRPO for 200 steps, four seeds each, otherwise following the setup of Hübotter et al. (2026) ; we provide our hyperparameters in Section E.1 . Figure 3 shows Qwen3-8B; results for the other two models and tables of accuracies are in Section D.1 . SDPO does not improve on new problems. Over 200 steps, GRPO improves test_unseen by 3.7 3.7 , 4.9 4.9 , and 2.6 2.6 points on Qwen3-8B, Qwen3-14B, and Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, whereas SDPO changes it by − 2.5 -2.5 , − 0.5 -0.5 , and − 9.9 -9.9 points. The disparity is largest on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, where SDPO ends 13.1 13.1 points below GRPO ( 21.0 21.0 vs. 34.1 34.1 ). In summary, we find that mimicking a privileged teacher does not generalize to new problems. SDPO does generalize to held-out test cases. SDPO’s gains on train_seen largely carry over to train_unseen ( + 23.1 +23.1 vs. + 18.4 +18.4 on Qwen3-8B, + 22.5 +22.5 vs. + 17.2 +17.2 on Qwen3-14B, and + 18.3 +18.3 vs. + 16.7 +16.7 on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct), retaining 76–91% of the gain compared with 81–103% for GRPO. SDPO therefore overfits at the level of training problems instead of at the level of unit tests, and produces fewer distinct solutions per training problem than GRPO ( Figure 1 ). We hypothesize this is because a problem’s test cases check the same specification, so a program that passes the seen test cases is usually correct and passes the held-out ones too. This reconciles our results with those of Hübotter et al. (2026) ; indeed, evaluating on train_seen and train_unseen at 80 steps across all three models, we find that SDPO beats GRPO. On Qwen3 models, GRPO overtakes SDPO on training problems with longer training. SDPO improves faster early on but then slows, while GRPO keeps improving and overtakes it after ∼ \sim 160 steps on both train_seen and train_unseen . At 200 steps on Qwen3-8B, GRPO scores 50.9 50.9 on train_seen and 46.2 46.2 on train_unseen , versus 48.9 48.9 and 44.0 44.0 for SDPO; on Qwen3-14B, GRPO scores 54.1 54.1 and 49.2 49.2 , versus 51.9 51.9 and 45.4 45.4 . The ∼ \sim 80-step comparison of Hübotter et al. (2026) therefore does not reflect performance at convergence—at 80 steps, GRPO is still improving and SDPO’s advantage disappears with further training. In Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, SDPO continues to outperform GRPO on training problems.

Hübotter et al. (2026) evaluate SDPO on SciKnowEval multiple-choice science questions ( Feng et al., 2024 ) and ToolAlpaca ( Tang et al., 2023 ) , with teachers conditioned on correct neighboring solutions. Unlike more difficult math and coding tasks, where reaching the answer requires multi-step derivation, answers in these domains can be directly produced by choosing among four options or emitting an API call whose structure is largely determined by the prompt. We train Qwen3-8B with SDPO and GRPO on each domain for 200 200 steps over four seeds, following their settings, and evaluate each trained model on the held-out validation set of all five domains; we report our hyperparameters in Section E.1 and full training curves in Section D.2 . SDPO improves on the training domain faster, but GRPO converges to comparable accuracies. In biology, chemistry, and physics, SDPO improves in-domain accuracy faster than GRPO early in training, while GRPO improves gradually over all 200 200 steps ( Figure 6 ). By step 200 200 , the two methods are within one standard deviation of each other in biology, material, and physics (SDPO vs. GRPO: 52.5 52.5 vs. 51.0 51.0 , 73.5 73.5 vs. 76.2 76.2 , and 73.1 73.1 vs. 72.4 72.4 ); the only clear differences are chemistry, where SDPO leads ( 77.7 77.7 vs. 68.9 68.9 ), and tool use, where GRPO leads ( 53.5 53.5 vs. 66.3 66.3 ) ( Table 1 ). Averaged over the five domains, both methods reach similar in-domain accuracy ( 66.1 66.1 for SDPO and 67.0 67.0 for GRPO, up from 49.6 49.6 for the base model). SDPO degrades out of domain, while GRPO does not. Training SDPO on any of the four science domains lowers average out-of-domain accuracy by 7.1 7.1 to 16.6 16.6 points, whereas GRPO slightly improves it ( + 0.9 +0.9 to + 1.6 +1.6 ; Table 1 ). Training on tool use is the exception, with SDPO slightly improving out-of-domain accuracy ( + 0.9 +0.9 ), with GRPO slightly lowering it ( − 2.1 -2.1 ). The drops are largest when evaluating on material, physics, and tool use, where SDPO’s accuracy peaks early in training and then declines steadily ( Figure 6 ). SDPO’s in-domain gains thus come at the cost of out-of-domain performance that policy-gradient training generally preserves.

sections.heading: 4.3 OPSD gains depend on thinking mode transfer, not privileged information
sections.text: OPSD ( Zhao et al., 2026a ) reports gains on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25 ( Mathematical Association of America, 2024 ; Balunović et al., 2025 ) by distilling a thinking-on Qwen3 teacher conditioned on a reference solution z z into the same model with thinking off ( Appendix C ). The teacher thus differs from the student in two ways: it sees z z , and it thinks. We therefore seek to isolate the influence of the content of z z with the teacher thinking mode. If OPSD gains come from conditioning on z z , replacing it with the reference solution of a different problem or removing it entirely should degrade performance. Setup. Following Zhao et al. (2026a) , we train on OpenThoughts ( Guha et al., 2025 ) math problems, each paired with a reference solution. We fix the student to thinking-off and ablate the teacher’s thinking mode (on or off) and its privileged information: the problem’s own reference solution (ref z z ), no reference solution (no z z ), or the reference solution of a different problem (shuffled z z ). The teacher template is otherwise fixed, so the three differ only in the content of z z . Zhao et al. (2026a) train Qwen3-1.7B to 8B with OPSD for 100 steps and compare against thinking-on GRPO (500 steps) and SFT (100 steps). To evaluate fully converged performance, we train OPSD and SFT for 200 steps and GRPO, with thinking on and off, for 500 steps, and evaluate on the same datasets with thinking on and off. As Shenfeld et al. (2026) ; Hübotter et al. (2026) suggest self-distillation works better for larger models, we also test Qwen3-14B and a second model family, Olmo-3-7B-Instruct. As the latter has no thinking toggle, we instead compare two teachers given the same privileged information: the student itself (self-distillation) and Olmo-3-7B-Think, a separately trained thinking model from the same family (cross-model distillation), which cleanly separates privileged information from thinking-mode transfer. We report Qwen3-8B validation results in Table 2 , remaining results and statistics in Section D.3 , and hyperparameters in Table 24 . Table 2: Qwen3-8B training methods evaluated under avg@12 with thinking-on and thinking-off evaluation. OPSD think/no think denote whether teacher thinking was on during OPSD training. This cosine similarity metric is also loosely motivated by Section 3.1 ): if the self-conditioned teacher approximates π ∗ \pi^{*} ( Equation 4 ), as Shenfeld et al. (2026) assume, the distillation gradient should follow the policy gradient on the training problems. Here we ask the analogous question on held-out problems, where the policy gradient is the direction that improves generalization. Setup. Practical self-distillation losses differ from the idealized objectives of Proposition 3.1 : they use other divergences such as Jensen–Shannon, per-token clipping, top- k k logit approximations, and EMA teachers ( Equation 3 ), so rather than testing the proposition’s equality directly, we test a consequence: a method whose teacher approximates the optimal teacher should update the model in the same direction as the policy gradient. We therefore measure the cosine similarity between each method’s training gradient and a reference , the GRPO gradient on held-out problems, which is the policy gradient direction that increases reward on new problems. To a first order approximation, a small step along a method’s gradient increases held-out reward if its cosine similarity with the reference is positive, and decreases it if negative. All gradients are estimated at the base model: on-policy RL favors high-reward policies that stay close to the base model in KL ( Shenfeld et al., 2025 ) , so we test whether the teacher is KL-optimal relative to the base model. We use the same setup as Section 4.1 and Section 4.3 : for math, methods train on OpenThoughts and the reference is GRPO nothink {}_{	ext{nothink}} on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25 (held-out math policy gradient); for LiveCodeBench v6, methods train on train_seen and the reference is GRPO on test_unseen . We report our complete results in Section D.6 . Since cosine similarity is a nonlinear function of the pooled gradients and we estimate gradients over four seeds, we estimate its error with a leave-one-seed-out jackknife; we detail our gradient estimation method in Section E.3 . OPSD points away from the held-out math policy gradient. Across Qwen3-1.7B to 14B, GRPO nothink {}_{	ext{nothink}} is the only method with positive cosine similarity with the held-out policy gradient on every model ( + 0.018 +0.018 to + 0.166 +0.166 ), and clearly so on Qwen3-8B and 14B ( + 0.118 ± 0.050 +0.118\pm 0.050 and + 0.166 ± 0.029 +0.166\pm 0.029 ; Tables 4 and 18 ). In contrast, all 24 24 OPSD variants have negative cosine similarity ( − 0.205 -0.205 to − 0.067 -0.067 ). On Qwen3-8B, the six variants lie between − 0.172 -0.172 and − 0.157 -0.157 , within each other’s error bars. Notably, OPSD with a thinking-on teacher points away from the held-out policy gradient despite its large thinking-off gains ( Table 2 ): rather than moving the student towards its own high-reward solutions like policy gradients, it improves performance by matching the teacher’s thinking style ( Section 4.3 ). Instead, on Olmo-3-7B-Instruct, GRPO and all six OPSD variants have small positive cosine similarity ( + 0.026 +0.026 to + 0.062 +0.062 ), but their jackknife errors ( 0.021 0.021 to 0.054 0.054 ) are comparable to the values themselves, so none are clearly resolved from zero ( Table 19 ). SDPO gradients are less aligned than GRPO gradients. On LiveCodeBench v6, SDPO is less aligned with the held-out policy gradient than GRPO on all three models, and points away from it on Qwen3-8B ( Table 4 ). These results are consistent with SDPO’s failure to improve test_unseen accuracy ( Section 4.1 ), suggesting the self-distillation objective is only weakly correlated with generalizable reward maximization. Self-distillation gradients have low variance but are misaligned. OPSD and SDPO gradients are nearly identical across seeds: their gradient noise scale ( McCandlish et al., 2018 ) , a normalized measure of variance across seeds where 0 0 is noiseless ( Section E.3 ), is at most 0.05 0.05 , versus 1.97 1.97 to 4.11 4.11 for GRPO across all models (see Section D.6 ). Self-distillation thus delivers the low-variance signal it promises, but that signal does not point along the held-out policy gradient: the self-conditioned teacher does not approximate the optimal teacher of Proposition 3.1 .

sections.heading: 5 Limitations
sections.text: Our experiments are limited to the Qwen3 and Olmo model families and the SDPO and OPSD self-distillation recipes. We do not address the more recent developments on self-distillation techniques, which include harnesses ( Zhao et al., 2026b ) , contrastive formulations ( Pan et al., 2026 ) , or more complex aggregation of feedback from neighboring rollouts ( Yu et al., 2026 ) , which may combat the limitations of these self-distillation methods. Moreover, we focus on verifiable domains and acknowledge that self-distillation has use cases in non-verifiable settings ( Buening et al., 2026 ) .

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: We show that the gains attributed to privileged self-distillation either do not generalize or do not come from privileged information. SDPO’s improvements on LiveCodeBench v6 are confined to problems seen during training, and its gains in other domains are come at the cost of out-of-distribution performance. OPSD’s math gains rely on thinking-mode transfer, with privileged information having little effect. Finally, self-distillation gradients do not align with the policy gradient on held-out problems, indicating that the self-conditioned teacher does not approximate the optimal teacher. Together, these results highlight the need to develop principled reinforcement learning methods that can exploit privileged information.

sections.heading: Appendix A Extended related works
sections.text: We divide existing work on the limitations of self-distillation techniques into the following: Empirical re-evaluations. Wang et al. (2026) demonstrate that SDPO struggles to generalize to out-of-distribution domains, and fail in continual learning settings where GRPO succeeds. Kaur et al. (2026) highlight that self-distillation degrades thinking-models; with previous works primarily focusing on instruction-tuned models. Concurrent to our work, Shrestha and Tessier (2026) ; Zhang et al. (2026) ; Ichihara et al. (2026) show that OPSD does not rely on privileged information, but on thinking-mode transfer. In contrast to these works, we provide our results with an exact reproduction of SDPO and OPSD training and evaluating settings, and we ask whether SDPO’s gains in other domains reflect improvements in reasoning. Token-level symptoms. Kim et al. (2026) ; Kaur et al. (2026) ; Pan et al. (2026) ; Harne et al. (2026) show that self-distillation losses concentrate on tokens which express uncertainty and have high entropy. This results in a suppression of the student’s backtracking behavior and collapse in response lengths. Instead, we focus on the positive results reported by OPSD, and find through token-level diagnoses and response length metrics, that performance improvements relate to thinking-mode transfer. Sequence-level diagnoses. Nguyen et al. (2026) develop statistics that indicate that the self-conditioned teacher cannot differentiate between correct and incorrect solutions generated by the student. Harne et al. (2026) present analogous results, showing that the self-conditioned teacher is greatly biased towards the reference solution it is provided, mirroring Yang et al. (2026) ’s results indicating that the teacher leaks privileged information. On the other hand, we diagnose whether the self-conditioned teacher approximates the optimal KL-regularized model, which is an assumption behind prior self-distillation work ( Shenfeld et al., 2026 ) . Remedies. Pan et al. (2026) and Yang et al. (2026) retain GRPO as a learning signal and use the self-conditioned teacher only to modulate its per-token advantages. Because these methods do not rely on the self-distillation loss alone, which is the setting we study, they fall outside the scope of this work. Their reliance on GRPO is consistent with Harne et al. (2026) , who question whether the self-distillation objective on its own, without such auxiliary machinery, yields any performance gains at all.

sections.heading: Appendix C Qwen3 thinking modes
sections.text: Qwen3 models support a thinking and a non-thinking mode in the same model ( Qwen Team, 2025 ) . For the flagship models (Qwen3-32B and Qwen3-235B-A22B), the two modes are merged during post-training ( Thinking Mode Fusion ) by fine-tuning on a mixture of “thinking” and “non-thinking” data. The smaller models (Qwen3 0.6B to 14B and Qwen3-30B-A3B) inherit both of these modes through supervised fine-tuning and on-policy-distillation from the flagship models. Concretely, in thinking mode, the model reasons inside a <think> … </think> block before responding. The mode is toggled via the enable_thinking argument of the chat template. When it is set to False, an empty think block is prefilled in the assistant turn: <|im_start|>assistant <think> </think> In non-thinking mode, the model is trained to respond directly after this empty thinking block.

sections.heading: Appendix E Implementation details
sections.text: All our experiments are run were run with 8xH100 nodes (with no multi-node parallelism), primarily leveraging the vLLM inference engine ( Kwon et al., 2023 ) . We run our experiments on top of the OPSD codebase written in TRL ( von Werra et al., 2020 ) and the SDPO codebase which uses veRL ( Sheng et al., 2024 ) . Our SDPO LCBv6 runs train for ∼ \sim 40 hours, while the SDPO science and tool use jobs took ∼ \sim 3 hours. OPSD runs took up to ∼ \sim 2 hours and GRPO runs on the OpenThoughts dataset took up to ∼ \sim 6 hours. OPSD thinking-on evaluations took up to ∼ \sim 2.5 hours per dataset and OPSD thinking-off evaluations took up to ∼ \sim 1 hour per dataset. Our gradient similarity analyses took up to ∼ \sim 2 hours per training setting.

sections.heading: E.3 Gradient similarity analysis
sections.text: We record each method’s gradients by running its training loop from the base model with learning rate zero, so the weights never change, and averaging the gradients over all iterations of each run for downstream computation. We use the hyperparameters of Tables 22 and 24 , with two exceptions: GRPO uses num_iterations = 1 =1 , since at learning rate zero a second pass over the same rollouts gives the same gradient, and we record gradients with respect to all parameters rather than the LoRA adapters (for the math results), since LoRA’s zero-initialized matrices may lead to poorly defined gradient behavior. We run 64 iterations per seed for OPSD on OpenThoughts and 8 for SDPO on LiveCodeBench v6, with four seeds per method.
